topics.topic: Classification when an opened metadata-nonempty file immediately reaches EOF
questions: If the metadata size is nonzero but the opened file immediately reaches end of file with no bytes, does A1 order 1 still apply as A1 explicitly says, or may order 1 be decided only from the pre-open metadata as this passage says?
When metadata reports a non-empty file but the opened file reaches EOF with no bytes, is A1 order 1 still applied after opening, or are only A1 orders 3 to 6 available after opening?

quotes:
When the listing reaches an entry, one metadata reading of its path, without following a link, decides
that it is a regular file and gives its listed size and modification time. Orders 1 and 2 are first
decided by that size, before the file is opened. A file is then read once, up to one byte past the
imported `MAX_SOURCE_BYTES` constant: reaching that byte is order 4, and the read stops there. A read that
reaches the end of the file with no bytes is order 1.

Condition 1 is decided from the name and the metadata of its path before
the file is opened. Condition 2 decides A1 orders 1 and 2 from that same metadata, before the file is
opened, and its other orders and conditions 3 and 4 from the opening on.
judgement.divergence: One passage classifies an empty read after opening as A1 order 1 and therefore EMPTY; the other confines A1 orders 1 and 2 to pre-open metadata, allowing the delivery caller to receive a later failure such as UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT.
judgement.why: The passages assign the post-open zero-byte case to different parts of the ordered decision.

witness.initial: A regular source file has a nonzero metadata size, valid image content and no existing placement.
events: The caller requests delivery with the source id of the original content.
The deliverer reads the nonzero path metadata.
Syncthing truncates the file before it is opened.
The deliverer opens it and immediately reaches end of file without reading any bytes.
outcomes: The explicit empty-read rule makes the result A1 order 1, and the caller receives the EMPTY member of PlacementFailure.
Because orders 1 and 2 were decided only from the nonzero metadata, post-open processing proceeds to later orders and can return the UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT member of PlacementFailure.
basis:
One call delivers one photo, named by `name`, a relative path in the form a scan reports, and
   `source_id`. The service keeps no memory of earlier scans: it judges the name and the file when the call
   runs. The named file is read once, and the bytes that were read are the bytes judged, hashed and prepared.

Syncthing may change the folder during a scan, so a scan is not a view of one instant. Each rule applies
to what its step finds when it runs, and the next scan sees the folder as it then stands. A file that
changes while it is read is judged by the bytes that were read, once, without a retry. Syncthing replaces
a finished file by renaming a new one over it; a later delivery judges what it then reads under A3 rule 5.

topics.topic: Datetime representation and precision of filesystem modification times
questions: What exact datetime representation and precision must be produced from the filesystem modification time?

In what exact datetime representation and precision is the filesystem modification time retained and converted when it supplies the fallback photo time: UTC-aware or UTC without an offset, and are subsecond or nanosecond digits preserved, truncated or rounded?

quotes:
The photo date is delivered as UTC without an offset, as the Client Portal stores it. A camera
time with no offset is read in the configured time zone. A local time that occurs twice is the
first occurrence, and a local time that does not exist is read with the offset in force before
the clock change. A modification time is an absolute instant converted to UTC.

The current time is a `datetime` in UTC without an offset, with microsecond precision and no
   rounding, written in ISO 8601 form. It sets `marked_at`.

A file's modification time is converted to the same form before it is compared or delivered, dropping
   any fraction finer than a microsecond toward the earlier instant.
judgement.why: The rules require naive UTC at microsecond precision and truncate finer fractions toward the earlier instant.

topics.topic: Source of the file-modification fallback time and number of metadata readings during delivery

quotes:
When the listing reaches an entry, one metadata reading of its path, without following a link, decides
that it is a regular file and gives its listed size and modification time.

Condition 1 is decided from the name and the metadata of its path before
the file is opened. Condition 2 decides A1 orders 1 and 2 from that same metadata, before the file is
opened, and its other orders and conditions 3 and 4 from the opening on.

The photo moment is the first usable value of: EXIF `DateTimeOriginal`, EXIF `DateTime`, then

A file's modification time is converted to the same form before it is compared or delivered, dropping

judgement.divergence: One implementation uses the pre-open path-metadata time and performs no later metadata read; another obtains modification time from the opened file or a later metadata read, so the owner and Portal can receive different photo dates for the same bytes.
judgement.why: The rules define the conversion and identify a pre-open metadata value but do not say that this value is the fallback photo instant or prohibit another metadata reading during delivery.

witness.initial: A regular image without a usable camera date has modification time T1 and no placement.

The deliverer reads pre-open path metadata and obtains T1.
Another actor changes only the modification time to T2 while the unchanged image is being read.

basis:
One call delivers one photo, named by `name`, a relative path in the form a scan reports, and
   `source_id`. The service keeps no memory of earlier scans: it judges the name and the file when the call
   runs. The named file is read once, and the bytes that were read are the bytes judged, hashed and prepared.

Syncthing may change the folder during a scan, so a scan is not a view of one instant. Each rule applies
to what its step finds when it runs, and the next scan sees the folder as it then stands. A file that
changes while it is read is judged by the bytes that were read, once, without a retry. Syncthing replaces
a finished file by renaming a new one over it; a later delivery judges what it then reads under A3 rule 5.

- INV-01: after a scan, a placement, a repeated placement and a mark, the source folder holds the same files with the same bytes, modification times and modes (`test_no_operation_changes_the_source_folder`).
judgement.divergence: One test observes source-tree mutation events and fails on transient file or directory changes; another compares only final files and their listed attributes and passes an implementation that creates and removes a temporary file, which Syncthing or a filesystem audit can notice.

topics.topic: Source, representation, and reading count for PublicationMark.marked_at
questions: What is the source and representation of marked_at, and how many readings does one mark operation take?

quotes:
The same `photo_id` again answers `replayed` with the first mark. Another `photo_id` is refused
   with `publication_conflict` and nothing changes.

Only a mark reads it, once, after the token, the request form and the identifiers are accepted and
   before the connection is examined or the project lock is taken. A mark refused before that point does
   not read it. A mark refused after it, and a replayed mark, have read it and write nothing. Scan, delivery
   and the health answer never read it.

The current time is a `datetime` in UTC without an offset, with microsecond precision and no
   rounding, written in ISO 8601 form. It sets `marked_at`.

- INV-08: a repeated mark keeps the first `marked_at`, and another `photo_id` is refused (`test_marking_again_changes_nothing_and_another_photo_is_refused`). A mark for a source placed only in another project is refused (`test_a_photo_that_was_not_placed_cannot_be_marked`).
judgement.why: A mark reads the system clock once, stores that naive UTC microsecond value without rounding, and replay returns the unchanged first mark despite performing its own non-stored clock read.
